prize_parts.citation: for establishing that biomolecular condensates form by liquid-liquid phase separation, a physical-chemical principle of intracellular organisation

statement.case_for: I keep B019 as my preferred configuration after re-reading the full exchange. The scientific case is unchanged: Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules behave as liquid droplets that dissolve, fuse and drip, and Rosen's work on multivalent interactions gave the quantitative phase-diagram description in which valency and affinity set the threshold for demixing. Together they replaced a vague notion of cellular compartments with a thermodynamic one, which is the kind of reduction to general physical-chemical principles that I value. In answer to the chair's question about what is beyond dispute, I would point to three things: purified, multivalent proteins and RNAs demix into dense liquid phases at defined concentrations in vitro, with measurable phase boundaries; P granules and the nucleolus show liquid-like dynamics in living cells; and the principle has reorganised how people ask about stress granules and neurodegeneration-linked aggregation. What remains contested is how many cellular condensates are functionally phase-separated at native expression levels, and I would keep that out of the citation. I narrowed my wording to put the principle first and not the claim that every condensate is physiologically essential.
statement.case_against: Round 1 sharpened rather than removed my reservations. Linke questions timing, and I concede that physiological scope is unsettled. Nobody other than me prefers B019, so on committee support it is clearly behind B011 (four members) and B068 (two). I do not treat that as decisive, but it means I should be honest that the scientific case rests on novelty of concept against maturity of evidence, and a majority may reasonably weigh maturity more heavily. Credit is also real trouble: the experimental discovery (Hyman, Brangwynne) and the theory and sequence grammar (Rosen, Pappu, Mittag) cannot be cut at three without leaving out decisive contributors. And the committee could fairly say this field sits closer to cell biology than to chemistry.

responses.point: Linke finds the polymer-physics framing attractive but is cautious on timing, asking which observations about condensates are now beyond dispute, and shares the worry that physiology may be the natural home.
responses.response: The fair answer is that the in vitro physical chemistry is beyond dispute: multivalent macromolecules demix at defined concentrations and the phase diagrams are reproducible and predictive. The liquid character of P granules and the nucleolus in living cells is also well documented. What is not settled is the functional role of many reported condensates at endogenous expression, and I would not want the citation to claim it. I accept that this is a narrower, more defensible claim than the one I made in round 1, and that it leaves the field younger than B011 by decades. I have not persuaded you on timing and I do not expect to, but I now state the claim in the form I think the evidence supports.

responses.point: Somfai holds B011 first for its clean two-name attribution and conceptual clarity (amine binding, deprotonation, reductive elimination from Pd-amido complexes), and acknowledges the 2010 overlap and Kosugi's tin-amide precursor.
responses.response: His mechanistic description persuades me that C-N coupling is more than a heteroatom variant of C-C coupling, since the rate-limiting steps and the ligand design problem differ, and I withdraw the suggestion in round 1 that it is merely a late increment in synthetic methodology. My remaining question is one of balance and not merit. I accept his view that Kosugi belongs in the narrative and not in the citation, because Buchwald and Hartwig are the ones who made the reaction general. I would not oppose B011, and I list it as my first alternative. I do not accept that breadth of support settles the comparison with a new organising principle, but I will not claim B019 is better supported than it is.

responses.point: Zou proposes a two-part prize pairing B011 (Buchwald, Hartwig) with nitrogenase structure (B003, Rees alone), within the three-person limit.
responses.response: I see the logic of two mature, distinct achievements, but I find the nitrogenase part hard to defend: giving the structure to Rees alone leaves out Einsle's high-resolution carbide structure and the biochemistry of Seefeldt, Dean and Ribbe, as he concedes himself, while the mechanism and N2 binding site are still unresolved. A part I cannot attribute cleanly weakens the whole configuration. If a two-part prize were needed to widen representation beyond synthesis, I would rather see the second part carry a physical-chemical or biophysical concept, but the three-name cap makes that impossible with B011, which is why I keep my position single-part.

responses.point: Aili prefers B068 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that it is the only candidate that both founded a design principle and spread across chemical biology and the clinic, with the widest opening support.
responses.response: I agree it has the broadest base and is the strongest chemical-biology case, and it remains my second alternative. I still would not equate breadth with strength, since he himself notes the rankings were mostly third, fourth or eighth. The decisive point for me is the one he and Chabes disagree on: Handa and Ito's cereblon glue work and the Crews and Deshaies PROTAC work are arguably separate achievements, so choosing Handa or Ciulli is a choice of what the prize is for. I would want one citation that states the principle (recruiting the ubiquitin-proteasome system by a designed molecule) before I could support any three-name set.

responses.point: Chabes prefers B068 with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, arguing the chemistry is mature even though no degrader is approved, and that ternary-complex structures and cooperativity make the approach rational and general.
responses.response: His argument that ternary-complex structures and quantified cooperativity make the mechanism chemically well characterised is the point that moves me most toward B068, and I agree that the absence of an approved drug should not by itself defer it. The unresolved issue is the lineage question: with Ciulli beside Crews and Deshaies the molecular-glue strand is excluded, with Handa the VHL strand is. I can support B068 as a second choice, but I still do not see which three names make the citation exact.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards in-cell phase separation as established enough for a Chemistry prize now, given that physiological relevance of many condensates is still debated.
Whether three names can be cut among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag without excluding a decisive contributor.
Whether B011 is the more defensible choice on maturity and attribution, and whether I give novelty of concept more weight than the rest of the committee should.
Whether a single citation can cover both the PROTAC and molecular-glue strands of B068, and with which third name.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I share Lund University with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my work on lipids, interfaces and amyloid is thematically close to B019 and B063 and overlaps with Brzezinski and Aili on membranes and self-assembly. These are field proximities, not personal ties, and I have no recorded collaboration with any listed candidate. Round 1 did not change this disclosure.
